name: Vasantha
definition: Vasantha is a composite portrait of a Lingayat woman running a small groundnut oil-pressing operation in Deodurga taluk, Raichur district, Kalyana Karnataka. She represents the region's women entrepreneurs balancing agricultural trade, household management, and the challenges of educating children in a district that ranks among Karnataka's most backward under the Nanjundappa Committee framework.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Vasantha runs a small oil-pressing unit inherited from her father-in-law in the Deodurga market yard, where farmers bring groundnut and sunflower seed from the surrounding dryland taluks. She opens the shop by seven in the morning, sorting seed by quality, running the mechanical expeller, and bottling oil in recycled plastic containers for local retail and hotel supply. Her husband drives their second-hand tempo to deliver orders across Deodurga and Lingsugur taluks. The work is seasonal: peak demand runs from November through February after the kharif groundnut harvest, then slows until sunflower arrives in April. Income fluctuates sharply with seed prices and diesel costs for transport. A good month brings fifteen to eighteen thousand rupees in profit; a bad one barely covers the electricity bill and labour for the helper boy they employ during harvest season. Vasantha keeps accounts in a lined notebook, tracking credit extended to repeat customers and outstanding payments, a constant worry in a trade built on trust and delayed settlement.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Vasantha lives in a two-room house behind the oil mill with her husband, two daughters aged thirteen and nine, and her mother-in-law, who is seventy and partially blind from untreated cataracts. Her husband's younger brother migrated to Hyderabad for construction work and sends money irregularly. Vasantha married at nineteen, shortly after completing her second PUC, and her mother-in-law often reminds her that she studied longer than most women in the family. Gender roles are negotiated daily: Vasantha manages the shop's money and customer relations, but her husband makes all major business decisions and handles travel. She wakes at five to prepare breakfast and tiffin for the children, works at the mill until midday, then returns home to cook lunch before reopening in the afternoon. Her mother-in-law helps with housework when her eyesight permits, but cannot be left alone. Vasantha's elder daughter has begun to resent the expectation that she will cook and care for her grandmother after school, a tension Vasantha tries to mediate without openly contradicting her mother-in-law.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Vasantha completed her second PUC at the government junior college in Deodurga town, an achievement she is quietly proud of; few women of her generation in the family went beyond Class 7. Her elder daughter attends the government high school in Deodurga and is preparing for her SSLC this year. Vasantha insists she will send her to PU college in Raichur city if she passes, despite her mother-in-law's objections about the cost and the propriety of a girl travelling so far. The younger daughter studies at the nearby Kannada-medium primary school. School fees are minimal under Anna Bhagya and other state schemes, but Vasantha spends nearly two thousand rupees a term on books, uniforms, and private tuition for mathematics and science, which the government high school barely covers. She dreams of her daughters studying for government jobs under the Article 371(J) local quota, a pathway she believes offers security this volatile trade cannot. The family hopes the elder girl will qualify for the Kalyana Karnataka Regional Development Board scholarship if she scores well, though Vasantha has heard stories of delayed payments and domicile-certificate disputes that make her anxious.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Vasantha's mother-in-law needs cataract surgery, but the waiting list at Raichur Institute of Medical Sciences stretches months, and private clinics in Raichur charge fees the family cannot afford upfront. Vasantha herself suffers recurring joint pain in her knees and lower back from years of standing at the mill and lifting seed sacks, but she rarely takes time off or consults a doctor. The family enrolled in Ayushman Bharat two years ago, though Vasantha is unsure what it covers and has never needed to use the card. Her daughters are healthier than she was at their age, but the younger one had a prolonged fever last monsoon that required a week of private-clinic visits and antibiotics, costing nearly three thousand rupees. Vasantha worries about fluoride in the borewell water they drink at home; neighbours speak of dental staining and bone pain, and a government survey team visited once but never returned with results. The 108 ambulance took her mother-in-law to Raichur during a fainting episode last year, but the emergency-room wait was six hours, and they were sent home with no follow-up. Vasantha sees health as something to manage with home remedies and prayer until a crisis forces hospital expense.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Vasantha's family belongs to the Lingayat community, and they observe Sharana tradition with daily prayers at the household shrine and annual visits to the Basavanna temple during Shivaratri. The local Lingayat mutt in Deodurga provides some social cohesion, organizing festivals and offering informal advice on disputes, though Vasantha herself rarely attends its gatherings, constrained by work and household duties. She speaks Kannada at home and in the market, though many of her Muslim customers speak Dakhni Urdu, and she has picked up enough to manage business greetings and accounts. Community ties are both a source of support and pressure: relatives expect loans, favours, and participation in life-cycle rituals that strain the family's time and budget. Vasantha draws strength from the memory of Basavanna's teachings on equality and work, and she quietly resents caste and gender hierarchies, though she seldom voices this openly. She respects her mother-in-law's authority at home and defers to her husband in public, while managing most practical decisions on her own. The shop's reputation depends on trust, and Vasantha is meticulous about fair weights and honest dealings, a pride she considers both spiritual duty and business necessity.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Vasantha has little direct interaction with local government beyond registering the oil mill for a trade licence and occasional visits from food-safety inspectors, who sometimes demand payments she considers unofficial. The family received a Gruha Jyothi electricity subsidy that reduced their household bill, though the mill's commercial connection does not qualify. Her elder daughter travels to school on the KKRTC bus under the Shakti free-travel scheme, a benefit Vasantha credits with making her willing to send the girl farther for PU college. She applied for a KKRDB scholarship for her daughter last year, but the process required multiple trips to the taluk office and a domicile certificate that took months to secure. She has heard of Article 371(J) guarantees for local jobs and education, but sees the benefits as captured by those with connections or the literacy to navigate bureaucracy. The idea of approaching a gram panchayat or taluk official for help feels remote; she expects officials to serve those who already have influence, not people like her.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Vasantha is proud that she runs her own business and educates her daughters, though she worries constantly about money, her mother-in-law's health, and whether the oil mill can sustain the family if seed prices spike or transport costs climb further. She blames poor rains, fluctuating groundnut prices, and the lack of government support for oilseed farmers for the trade's instability, and she resents that Raichur district is labelled backward without visible improvement in infrastructure or schools. Vasantha insists her daughters will not marry until they finish their education, but she feels the pressure of relatives and neighbours who think she is allowing them too much freedom. She is quietly proud of Kalyana Karnataka's Sharana heritage and the special constitutional status under Article 371(J), though she sees little of the promised funds reaching Deodurga. She worries that her elder daughter's ambition to study in Raichur city will expose her to risks Vasantha cannot control, yet she refuses to let fear trap the girl in the same limits she herself accepted. What Vasantha wants most is stability: reliable income, affordable healthcare for her mother-in-law, and a government job for at least one daughter, so the next generation does not have to wake each morning wondering if the market will cover the day's costs.
